extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Patent Office examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when material constitutes prior art and when a claim is anticipated under 35 U.S.C. 102, including public accessibility, dates of availability, admissions, use of multiple references, genus/species and ranges, and related evidentiary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of teachings relied upon for electronic publications
rubrics_metrics.description: An electronic publication may be relied upon for all that it would have reasonably suggested to one having ordinary skill in the art; if an electronic document is the abstract of a patent or printed publication relied upon in a 102/103 rejection, only the text of the abstract (and not the underlying document) may be relied upon to support the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If electronic and paper versions differ appreciably, each may need to be cited and relied upon as independent references based on what they disclose. See MPEP § 2121.01 and § 2123 for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet usage and citation procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet searching and documenting search strategies and the proper citation of electronic documents must follow the Internet Usage Policy and citation guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 904.02(c) for portions pertaining to Internet searching and documenting search strategies and MPEP § 707.05 for proper citation of electronic documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need to prove actual human inspection of a publication
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner need not prove someone actually looked at a publication when that publication is accessible to the public through a library or patent office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public accessibility alone can suffice to rely on a publication as prior art (cases: In re Wyer; In re Hall). Document accessibility practices (cataloging/shelving) can be used as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public accessibility criterion for theses and library materials
rubrics_metrics.description: A thesis placed in a university library may be prior art if sufficiently accessible to the public (e.g., indexed and shelved in a library).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess indexing/cataloging/shelving practices; compare In re Hall (accessible) with In re Cronyn (not accessible when only findable by student name). Consider whether a presumption can be raised that the portion of the public concerned with the art would know of the invention (In re Bayer). Historical Board decisions about single-copy shelving are noted but may be criticized. Use librarian affidavits and routine practices as evidence of accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral presentations as printed publications when written copies disseminated
rubrics_metrics.description: An orally presented paper can constitute a 'printed publication' if written copies are disseminated without restriction at a forum open to all interested persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: MIT v. AB Fortia (paper to 50–500 persons with written copies distributed without restriction counted as printed publication). Oral presentations or trade show demonstrations may also be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) as 'otherwise available to the public' (see MPEP § 2152.02(e)). A purely oral presentation without copies or slides is generally not a 'printed publication'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential internal documents are not printed publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents distributed internally within an organization that are intended to remain confidential are not 'printed publications.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be an existing policy of confidentiality or agreement within the organization; mere intent to remain confidential is insufficient. Cases: In re George; Garret Corp. v. United States; Northern Telecom v. Datapoint. Distribution to external commercial parties without restriction can make a document public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public display can constitute a printed publication even if transient
rubrics_metrics.description: A publicly displayed document may be a 'printed publication' even if displayed only for a few days and not disseminated by copies or indexed in a library/database, provided persons of ordinary skill could see and copy it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider (Klopfenstein): length of time exhibited, expertise of target audience, expectations about copying, and ease/simplicity of copying. Example: a 14‑slide poster displayed for ~3 cumulative days at industry events was held sufficiently publicly accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date of accessibility can be shown by routine business practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of routine business practices can establish the date on which a publication became accessible to the public; specific evidence showing when the specific document actually became available is not always necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use affidavits or documentation of normal indexing/cataloging/shelving or business practices (e.g., Constant v. AMD; In re Hall). Such routine practices can be sufficient to show accessibility before the critical date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date for mailed publications is date of receipt by public member
rubrics_metrics.description: A publication disseminated by mail is not prior art until it is received by at least one member of the public; effective date is when first person receives it, not the mailing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: In re Schlittler (magazine/technical journal effective as of date first received by a member of the public). Use corroborating evidence to establish receipt date if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions by applicant can constitute prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement by an applicant in the specification or made during prosecution identifying the work of another as 'prior art' is an admission that can be relied upon for anticipation and obviousness determinations, regardless of statutory category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must determine whether the subject matter identified as 'prior art' is applicant’s own work or another's; absent another credible explanation, treat it as work of another. Case law: Riverwood; Constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jepson-format claims imply admission of preamble subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafting a claim in Jepson format is taken as an implied admission that the subject matter of the preamble is prior art work of another, unless a credible reason for using Jepson format is provided or the preamble actually describes applicant's own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules per 37 CFR 1.75(e) and cases (In re Fout; In re Ehrreich; Reading & Bates). Applicant explanation (e.g., avoiding double patenting) can overcome the implication if credible and supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: IDS listing is not an admission of prior art or materiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere listing of a reference in an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) is not an admission that the reference is prior art or material to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Riverwood Int’l Corp. v. R.A. Jones & Co.; 37 CFR 1.97(h) explicitly states the filing of an IDS shall not be construed as an admission that the information cited is material to patentability as defined in § 1.56(b). Examiners should not treat IDS listings as admissions without other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requires a single reference teaching every element
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is anticipated only if each and every element of the claim is found, either expressly or inherently, in a single prior art reference under its broadest reasonable interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements must be arranged as required by the claim, but identity of terminology is not required (ipsissimis verbis test not required). If the claim covers alternatives, any known structure/composition within the claim scope can anticipate (Verdegaal; Brown v. 3M). See MPEP § 2114 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited use of multiple references in 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Normally only one reference should be used in a 35 U.S.C. 102 rejection, but multiple references or extrinsic evidence may be used in limited circumstances: (A) to prove the primary reference contains an 'enabled disclosure'; (B) to explain the meaning of a term used in the primary reference; or (C) to show that a characteristic not disclosed is inherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on extra references, explain their specific role (enablement, term meaning, inherency) and provide supporting evidence/case law (In re Samour; In re Donohue; Baxter Travenol; Continental Can). Examiners should not combine references to create a composite anticipatory disclosure except in these discrete contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra references to show primary reference has enabled disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: When the primary reference discloses the claimed subject matter identically, extra references may be used to show the primary reference had an enabled disclosure (e.g., methods of making).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation to combine is not required when the primary reference already teaches all claim elements; secondary patents/publications can be evidence that methods or enabling information were in the public’s possession (In re Samour; In re Donohue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra references/extrinsic evidence may explain but not expand meaning of terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence may be used to explain the meaning of a term used in the primary reference but may not be used to expand the meaning beyond what the primary reference reasonably conveys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use caution to avoid improperly broadening the primary reference's disclosure; supporting evidence (depositions, declarations, admissions) can show how a person of ordinary skill would understand a term (In re Baxter Travenol Labs.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use extrinsic evidence to show inherency only when necessarily present
rubrics_metrics.description: Extrinsic evidence can fill a gap in a reference to show an inherent characteristic, but the evidence must make clear that the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present in the thing described and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inherency findings require convincing evidence (test data, expert testimony) that the property inevitably results from the prior art disclosure (Continental Can; Atlas Powder; In re King). The critical date rules for extrinsic evidence may differ; see MPEP § 2124.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species anticipates genus
rubrics_metrics.description: A species disclosed in the prior art that falls within a claimed genus will anticipate the genus claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art discloses a specific species encompassed by a genus claim, anticipation follows (In re Slayter; In re Gosteli). Consider foreign priority issues where applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference expressly naming a species anticipates that species regardless of other species listed
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reference clearly names the claimed species, that disclosure anticipates the species claim no matter how many other species are named in the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even comprehensive listings (e.g., Merck Index analogies) that include the specific compound are sufficient to anticipate (Ex parte A; In re Sivaramakrishnan). Unexpected properties of a species disclosed among many may not avoid anticipation unless the reference fails to describe the species as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic disclosure can anticipate a species if the species can be 'at once envisaged'
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic disclosure will anticipate a claimed species when a person of ordinary skill would 'at once envisage' the specific species from the disclosure (i.e., be able to draw the structure or write the name immediately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider factual aspects: size of genus, limitation/delineation of substituents, presence of preferred embodiments, and whether PHOSITA could immediately envisage the species (Sanofi; Kennametal; In re Petering; In re Schauman). If significant selection/combination from lists is required, anticipation may not be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific prior-art example within a claimed range anticipates the range
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific example in the prior art that lies within a claimed numerical range anticipates the claimed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Titanium Metals v. Banner — actual data point within claimed compositional range anticipated the claim. Use explicit prior-art data points where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping or touching prior-art range anticipates only with 'sufficient specificity'
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prior-art range overlaps or touches a claimed narrow range but does not disclose a specific example within it, anticipation depends on whether the prior art discloses the claimed range with 'sufficient specificity' to constitute an anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate case-by-case; consider whether claimed range is narrow/critical and whether there is evidence of criticality or expected changes across ranges (ClearValue v. Pearl River Polymers; Atofina v. Great Lakes). If unclear, an examiner may issue a combined 102/103 rejection with reasoned statements for both anticipation and obviousness (Ex parte Lee). See MPEP § 2144.05 for obviousness of ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art very close but not overlapping does not anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art value or range that is very close to but does not overlap or touch the claimed range does not anticipate the claimed range; differences require § 103 analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation requires exact disclosure of what is claimed; when differences exist, rely on obviousness under § 103 rather than § 102 (Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner). Provide appropriate reasoning distinguishing the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations irrelevant to 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of secondary considerations (e.g., unexpected results, commercial success) is irrelevant to 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections and cannot overcome a rejection based solely on anticipation under § 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations are relevant to obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103) but not to novelty/anticipation determinations (In re Wiggins). Do not use commercial success or unexpected results to rebut a pure § 102 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arguments about nonanalogous art or teaching away not germane to § 102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that alleged anticipatory prior art is 'nonanalogous art' or 'teaches away' or is not recognized as solving the problem are not germane to a rejection under § 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such arguments are relevant to obviousness (§ 103) but do not affect a § 102 anticipation rejection (Twin Disc; In re Self). Examiners should focus on whether the reference discloses the claimed elements, not whether it is analogous or teaches away.
